bioOpener: I build automation and developer tools, and I care most about whether they actually keep working.
bioPoints: At OCBC I move fragile automations onto Playwright and give them shared logging and a health dashboard, so failures surface instead of hiding.
ROUTR ships with a 153-prompt eval set; DoorLens ships with a written limitations document. Where I cannot measure something, I say so.
I teach and facilitate at AI build workshops and hackathons. Explaining a system to a room is how I check that I understand it.

principles.title: Make the problem concrete
principles.body: Most stuck projects are stuck because nobody wrote down precisely what is wrong.

principles.title: Build the smallest credible version
principles.body: Small enough to finish, real enough that using it tells you something true.

principles.title: Improve from reality
principles.body: First contact with real people is the only honest feedback. Plan for it.

education.qualification: Diploma in Information Technology (Software and Applications)

experience.summary: Python automation, browser automation and observability for an enterprise technology team, inside a restricted corporate environment.
highlights: Migrated legacy coordinate- and image-based UI automations to Playwright browser automation, and standardised the Playwright setup across the team’s automation machines, removing a recurring source of breakage whenever an interface changed.
Designed and built a shared Python logging module (consistent format, levels and per-job log files) and am rolling it out across the team’s automation scripts in place of ad-hoc console output.

Designed and built an automation-health dashboard that discovers job logs, classifies each run as succeeded, failed or stalled from its most recent output, and summarises failures, so problems surface without anyone reading raw logs.
Maintain Python/pandas automations over large Excel datasets (100K+ rows), adding input validation so malformed or incomplete inputs fail loudly instead of producing wrong reports.
Diagnosed scheduling faults in production automations (unintended repeat runs, jobs that silently stopped running) and restored reliable scheduled execution.
Moved the team’s automation code into source control, inventoried and risk-classified existing scripts to prioritise hardening work, and ran a knowledge-sharing session on the new workflow.

headline: Software engineering student building automation, developer tooling and full-stack products
summary: Diploma in IT student at Singapore Polytechnic on a year-long engineering internship at OCBC, working on automation reliability and observability. Outside work I design and ship my own systems: an open-source routing layer for AI coding agents, an offline-first Android alarm app with a Kotlin reliability core, and full-stack web products with server-enforced access control.
experienceNote: Internship work is described at the level of engineering approach; system names and implementation details are omitted for confidentiality.
otherExperience: Event Assistant, Adecco — polling station operations, Singapore General Election 2025 (Apr – May 2025)

featuredProjects.name: ROUTR
featuredProjects.description: A routing layer for AI coding agents: small “router” skills that match a request to the right workflow and tell the agent what to read, in what order, and what to skip.
featuredProjects.challenge: Agents with dozens of installed skills pick the wrong one and burn their context window reading whole files.
built: 28 router skills with explicit “use when / not for” boundaries, and multi-step route plans capped at three steps with one router active at a time
A skill validator that runs in CI on every change, and an eval set of 153 prompts for measuring routing accuracy
featuredProjects.decision: Routing is decided from short skill descriptions alone, so the agent loads only the one full playbook it needs.
featuredProjects.outcome: MIT-licensed and installable with one command. The README reports 97–99% routing accuracy in blind model runs against the eval set, with the method published so it can be reproduced.

featuredProjects.name: Nudgio
featuredProjects.description: An Android alarm and reminder app that plays the user’s own media, designed to work with no backend and no Internet permission.
featuredProjects.challenge: An alarm has to fire on time even when the OS kills the app or the device restarts, and it has to fail gracefully when the chosen media file has been moved or deleted.
built: A Kotlin native core for scheduling, notifications and backup, exposed to a React Native UI through a typed native-module bridge
A layered TypeScript codebase with a mock bridge, so UI and service logic are testable without a device
featuredProjects.decision: Register only the single earliest alarm with the OS rather than one per reminder. Recorded with the project’s other design choices in 21 architecture decision records.
featuredProjects.outcome: In active development, built against a 23-document spec with a requirements traceability catalogue. Not yet released.

featuredProjects.name: StartupLink
featuredProjects.description: A closed network where students and verified student founders find each other.
featuredProjects.challenge: Trust is the product: founder status has to be verified, and each role may only see its own data.
built: Server-side founder verification in a Cloud Function, so it cannot be bypassed from the client
Role-based access enforced in Firestore security rules rather than in UI components
Multi-step onboarding that keeps partial progress across sessions
featuredProjects.decision: Authorisation lives in database rules, not the interface, so a modified client still cannot read another role’s data.
featuredProjects.outcome: Working MVP deployed publicly. No user numbers yet.

featuredProjects.name: LocalLoco
featuredProjects.description: Neighbourhood deal discovery: residents submit offers, volunteers moderate them, and QR redemption tells a business which promotions actually got used.
featuredProjects.challenge: Location queries that stay fast as data grows, and a moderation queue small enough for a few volunteers to clear.
built: A Next.js front end and a separate FastAPI service so each deploys independently
Location queries in PostGIS instead of application-side filtering
Separate submission and moderation stages so unreviewed content is never public, plus QR redemption tracking
featuredProjects.decision: Chose PostGIS early, which avoided a rewrite once real data existed.
featuredProjects.outcome: Running on its production domain with authentication in place.

featuredProjects.name: DoorLens
featuredProjects.description: Nebula X 2026 submission that classifies recorded train-door movements from sensor telemetry, with a tool for testing whether recording assumptions change a result.
featuredProjects.challenge: A small labelled dataset (110 training cycles) and no ground truth for the test set, so any claim about accuracy had to be honest.
built: A pipeline that validates uploaded CSVs, segments door cycles and runs a frozen classifier
A sensitivity probe that rescales or resamples a cycle and re-runs the same model to show whether the label holds
featuredProjects.decision: Models are frozen, hashed artefacts: uploads never retrain them, and every result carries the identity of the model that produced it.
featuredProjects.outcome: Submitted with a written limitations document and verification notes.

whyComputing: The question I keep coming back to is not whether software can be built, but how anyone knows it works. At OCBC that meant giving automations shared logging and a health dashboard, so a failure shows up instead of quietly producing a wrong report.

The same question runs through my own projects. ROUTR is measured against a 153-prompt evaluation set with a published method. DoorLens ships with a limitations document because its dataset was too small to claim more. Nudgio is an alarm, so it has to fire on time even after the operating system kills the app.

A diploma taught me to build. I want a degree to learn the parts I keep reaching for and do not yet have: the theory behind reliable systems, the mathematics behind evaluating models, and the discipline of proving rather than testing.

interests.why: How to design, test and observe systems so that failures are found by the system, not its users.
Building evaluation sets and methods that say honestly how well a model or agent performs, and where it does not.
